title: One Phenotype Can Hide Many Genes

scenes.tts: Cross two pure-breeding fruit fly lines. Both have white eyes. Yet the offspring can have ordinary red eyes. How can that be? A red eye needs pigment. Pigment is made in several steps, by the products of several genes. Losing any one step leaves the eye pale.
scenes.visual: Two white-eyed parent eyes cross into a question-mark box that turns into a red eye; below, a chain of steps makes pigment, and one step breaks so the eye goes pale.
scenes.narration: Cross two pure-breeding fruit fly lines. Both have white eyes. Yet the offspring can have ordinary red eyes. How can that be? A red eye needs pigment. Pigment is made in several steps, by the products of several genes. Losing any one step leaves the eye pale.

scenes.tts: Think of an assembly line with five stations. A broken station anywhere stops the product. So every breakdown looks the same at the end of the line. One line has station two broken. Another has station four broken. Borrow the working stations from each, and you get a working line. If both lines broke station two, borrowing helps nothing.
scenes.visual: A five-station line makes pigment; station 2 breaks and it goes pale; a second line breaks at station 4; a third line borrows the working stations and makes pigment; then both lines broken at station 2 give a borrowed line that stays pale.
scenes.narration: Think of an assembly line with five stations. A broken station anywhere stops the product. So every breakdown looks the same at the end of the line. One line has station two broken. scenes.tts: Now do the same with genes. Combine the two mutations in one diploid, one on each homologous chromosome. This arrangement is called trans. One mutation is in gene A. The other is in gene B. Each chromosome supplies the working allele that the other lacks. The phenotype is wild type. The mutations complement.
scenes.visual: Two homologous chromosomes carry genes A and B; gene A breaks on one, gene B on the other; the working copies light up and the result turns to wild type.
scenes.narration: Now do the same with genes. Combine the two mutations in one diploid, one on each homologous chromosome. This arrangement is called trans. One mutation is in gene A. The other is in gene B. Each chromosome supplies the working allele that the other lacks. The phenotype is wild type. The mutations complement.

scenes.tts: Now try two alleles of one gene, gene A, in trans. Each chromosome carries a broken copy of gene A. The diploid has no working copy. So it stays mutant. The mutations fail to complement. Mutations that fail to complement one another form a complementation group. In the simple model, that group is one gene.
scenes.visual: The result resets to a question mark; gene B is repaired and gene A is broken on both chromosomes; the result turns mutant; a box encloses both copies of gene A as one group.
scenes.narration: Now try two alleles of one gene, gene A, in trans. Each chromosome carries a broken copy of gene A. The diploid has no working copy. So it stays mutant. scenes.tts: Here is a worked problem. Six recessive white-eyed mutants are crossed in all fifteen pairs. Four pairs stay white: one and three, one and five, two and six, three and five. Mutant one fails with three and five. So one, three and five form a group. Mutant two fails only with six. Those two form a group. Mutant four complements all the others. That makes three complementation groups, so at least three genes. It is at least, because other genes may not have been hit.

scenes.tts: The test has a condition. Both mutations must be recessive. A dominant allele gives a mutant phenotype opposite any partner, so the trans result says nothing. For recessive mutations, keep this rule. In the simple model, wild type in trans means different genes. Mutant in trans means one gene.
scenes.visual: A dominant allele gives mutant against a normal partner, so the result says nothing; then two cards give the rule for recessive mutations in the simple model: wild type means different genes, mutant means one gene.
